title: Responsible for one another (Shevuot 39a)
hook: all Israel are responsible for one another

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: where you belong. Warmth, practice and place, and a teacher and a friend to make your own. What tied you a little tighter to your people? Today, what belonging costs. Day one thousand two hundred forty-nine.

Famine in Canaan, and the brothers have to go back to Egypt for grain. The ruler there has said: don't come back without your youngest brother, Benjamin. Their father Jacob refuses. He has already lost Joseph. Then Judah steps forward and says, in the King James words, "I will be surety for him; of my hand shalt thou require him." Put him on me. If he doesn't come home, the blame is mine. Later, in Egypt, Judah keeps that promise, offering to stay as a slave in Benjamin's place. Today's word comes from the same idea Judah stood on.
screen: `DON'T COME BACK WITHOUT HIM.` → `I WILL BE SURETY FOR HIM.` → `JUDAH KEEPS HIS WORD.`

segments.voice: Arevim. Guarantors. The singular is arev, the one who stands behind a debt. If the borrower can't pay, the arev pays. Turn it four ways. First, Judah. Readers hear the same Hebrew word in his promise to Jacob: I will be his guarantor. He puts his own life behind his brother's. Second, the Talmud. In tractate Shevuot, the rabbis read a hard verse from Leviticus about people stumbling over one another as they flee. They hear it as people stumbling through one another's failings, and they draw a principle: all Israel are guarantors, one for another. Kol Yisrael arevim zeh bazeh. When one person falls, the others are not bystanders. They co-signed. Third, what it does in practice. Rabbinic law uses this idea in a surprising place. Someone who has already said certain blessings can still say them again for another person who can't, because that other person's obligation is partly theirs. Your duty doesn't end at your own edge. Fourth, the weight and the comfort. The weight: on this view, no one can shrug at a neighbor's trouble and call it none of their business. The comfort: nobody in the community stands alone in front of the debt either. The streams we've met this block disagree about a great deal. A guarantor doesn't sign only for the borrowers they agree with. Judah didn't choose the brother who was easiest to protect. He chose the one who was in danger.
screen: `AREV: THE ONE WHO STANDS BEHIND THE DEBT.` · `JUDAH: PUT HIM ON ME.` · `ALL ISRAEL ARE GUARANTORS.` · `SAYING A BLESSING FOR ANOTHER.` · then, large: `RESPONSIBLE FOR ONE ANOTHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: help someone in your community. Settle, and breathe. Picture the people you call yours, and look for the one who is stumbling right now. A neighbor who's sick. A friend between jobs. A family that just lost someone. A new person nobody has spoken to yet. Ask what you could put your own hand behind: a meal, a ride, an introduction, a phone call that isn't rushed. Pick one, and make it something you'll really do. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. The bell holds the time.
Arevim. Guarantors: all Israel stand behind one another, like co-signers on a debt, as the Talmud teaches in Shevuot. Today's word.
Your line: responsible for one another. Today, do the one thing you chose for the person who is stumbling, before the day ends. Day one thousand two hundred forty-nine.

howItsDone: Jewish communities cite kol Yisrael arevim zeh bazeh when organizing help for members in need and for Jews in other places, and in Jewish law it allows one person to say certain blessings on another's behalf.

what a scholar hears: Shevuot 39a reads Leviticus 26:37 as stumbling through one another's failings, and readers hear the same word in Judah's surety.

notes: Root claim: Genesis 43:9 anokhi e'ervenu and arevim share the root ayin-resh-bet; stated as 'the same family of Hebrew words'. Confirm.
Shevuot 39a paraphrased: Leviticus 26:37 'ish be-achiv' read as 'one for the sin of another', yielding kol Yisrael arevim zeh bazeh. Confirm summary.
Application to blessings (one who has fulfilled may still say certain blessings for another, Rosh Hashanah 29a, with Rashi linking it to arevut): confirm wording 'certain blessings'.
Hook retells Genesis 42–44 in summary; Jacob's refusal (42:38) and Judah's offer (44:33).
